newsitem.title: USA: IVAX deal puzzles, HFS cheered - arbs.
newsitem.headline: IVAX deal puzzles, HFS cheered - arbs.

text.p: HFS Inc's plan to bolster and extend business lines with the acqusition of PHH Corp enjoyed wide support among Wall Street arbitrageurs soon after the deal was announced Monday.
But the rationale behind Monday's other large deal -- the merger of IVAX Corp and Bergen Brunswig Corp -- puzzled the arbs as shares of both fell on the news.
"It makes tremendous sense," an arb said of the $1.7 billion HFS-PHH stock swap deal, which values PHH at about $49.50 per share.
PHH rose 17-1/2 to 48-1/4 and HFS was up 3/8 at 74-1/2.

"HFS is in three line of business: vehicle fleet management -- and with HFS owning Avis there are a lot of synergies there -- the corporate relocation business, where PHH is number one and HFS is number two; and the mortgage business, which HFS is not in, but it makes a lot of sense with Century 21 (owned by HFS)," the arb said.
"And with HFS trading at 56 times earnings and PHH trading at a multiple of 20, it is sure to be accretive" to HFS earnings, he added.
Also, Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette analyst raised Mark Manson raised his 12-month target price for HFS to $100 per share from $90 and left unchanged his buy recommendation on the stock.
But early sentiment toward the announced combination of generic drug company IVAX and pharmaceutical distributor Bergen Brunswig was markedly different from the HFS deal.
"Boy, I don't like that at all, not for anyone," the arb said of the $1.65 billion stock-swap deal that valued IVAX shares below market value as of Friday's close.
In midsession trading, IVAX was off 2-3/4 to 13 while Bergen Brunswig tumbled four to 28-3/4.
"IVAX's problems started when there was significant price cutting in the generic drug industry and the company then ran into trouble with certain debt covenants," he said.

At the end of June, IVAX warned its second quarter earnings per share would be significantly below those of recent quarters, at about $0.06 to $0.08 per share, citing the factors referred to by the arbs.
Before this news, IVAX was trading between 25 and 30; it tumbled after the warnings to 15 and has not recovered.

"Bergen is taking on a major strategy shift, while they are not acquiring the highest quality company out there. Bergen now has to dramatically shift its focus and also clean up the problems at IVAX. It is going to take a lot to convince the analyst community that this makes sense," the second arb said.

This morning, IVAX announced a third quarter loss of $1.47 per share after a $104.3 million pre-tax charge related to the writedown of goodwill and other assets, versus a profit of $0.23 per share, while net revenues fell to $222.7 million from $310.2 million.
The Miami-based company also said it omitted its semiannual dividend for the 1996 second half and add $7 million to reserves related to a bankrupt customer.

"You have a distributor (Bergen) combining with a generics manufacturer (IVAX). Won't this impair the manufacturer's relationship with other distributors -- and what about the other drug companies that are being distributed through Bergen Brunswig?," the second arb asked.

"It's not too pretty; and remember the last guy (IVAX merger partner) could not get the vote in Norway," he said, referring to the unravelling one year ago of IVAX's merger agreement with Norway's Hafslund Nycomed A/S.

While the deal was expected to be backed by a majority of IVAX shareholders, the required two-third Hafslund shareholder support was found to be unlikely to be realized, so the vote was never held and the deal was called off.
-- Brendan Intindola, Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1734
